newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea could hit South with nuclear weapons-report.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea could hit South with nuclear weapons-report.

text.p: North Korea could destroy South Korea with nuclear and chemical weapons and would strike against Japan if the United States intervened, top Northern defector Hwang Jang-yop was quoted on Tuesday as saying in a report.
The Chosun Ilbo newspaper, known for its extensive South Korean intelligence sources, said Hwang wrote the report in August as he prepared to defect to the South.

Hwang, the highest-ranking official ever to flee communist North Korea, arrived in South Korea on Sunday via the Philippines, more than two months after seeking asylum in Seoul's consulate in Beijing on February 12.
"The North can turn the South into a sea of flame and annihilate it by using nuclear and chemical weapons and rockets," Hwang said in the report published on Tuesday.
"The North believes it will win a war and plans to annihilate Japan...if the United States meddles in it," he said.
Hwang, 74, once a confidant of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il, declared on arrival at an air base near Seoul that his mission was to stop Pyongyang from launching a war.

Officials in South Korea and its allies hope Hwang will spill secrets that could give them insights into the state of mind of the North Korean leadership as it slides into famine and economic catastrophe.
"The leadership in the North is now standing at a crossroads between staging the great tragedy in the history of our people by mobilising military force and surrendering," the August report said.
Hwang described the North Korean leader as a clever but radical, capricious and jealous person convinced that only he was capable of ruling his country.
"It is clear without any doubt that an historic tragedy is approaching our people," he said in the report.
The report also warned the North maintained a huge network of moles in the South and that the West must not expect the repressive system in the North to implode naturally.
Hwang's report urged the South and its allies not to push for reform in North Korea, saying it would help Pyongyang overcome its economic crisis and strengthen its military.
The United States and South Korea have been trying to convince North Korea to join landmark peace talks aimed at closing the books on the 1950-53 Korean War that ended with a now-fraying armistice.

South Korea's top negotiators in the proposed four-way peace talks said on Monday they were flying back to Seoul after they and U.S. officials failed to persuade North Korea to join the talks, which would also include China.

Although North Korean negotiators told U.S. and South Korean counterparts last Wednesday they essentially accepted the proposal, they conditioned that acceptance on demands for more food aid and lifting U.S. trade sanctions.
Since then, the North has failed to give its answer to the year-old U.S.-South Korean peace talks proposal. U.S. and South Korean officials said talks would continue.

In Washington, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the border between North and South is one of the most dangerous spots on Earth and the United States, with 37,000 troops there, remains ready to defend South Korea if needed.
